newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Cuban urges new U.S. policy towards Havana.
newsitem.headline: Cuban urges new U.S. policy towards Havana.

text.p: A vice-president of Cuba's ruling Council of State, Carlos Lage Davila, said on Tuesday the time had come for a new United States policy towards his country.

"Electoral tensions have already come to an end in this country. President William Clinton has been re-elected and another Democratic administration term has ensued. We believe the time has also come for a new U.S. policy toward Cuba," Lage said.

He was taking part in a General Assembly debate held annually since 1992 on the three-decade-old U.S. economic embargo against Cuba. The debate has ended each time with a lopsided majority adopting a resolution calling for an end to the ban. Last year's vote was 117-3, with 38 abstentions.
Even U.S. allies have supported the resolutions since they regard the embargo as violating their own sovereignty by subjecting them to U.S. laws and regulations.

Alluding to one of Clinton's favourite election images, Lage said: "Recent reports in this country refer to building a bridge into the 21st century. How can a bridge into the future be built if it is not possible to lay a much shorter bridge -- just 90 miles long, over which peace in the hemisphere may cross?" Cuba is about 90 miles (145 km) from the United States.
"We renew Cuba's readiness to discuss any issue with the United States. We require no precondition other than an absolute respect for our indefeasible right to freedom and sovereignty," Lage said.

Referring to the Helms-Burton Act, the most recent U.S. law aimed at penalising those who trade with Cuba, he said it violated international law and the U.N. Charter because of its "extraterritorial, unilateral and coercive nature."

The law allows U.S. citizens who were Cuban nationals before the 1959 Communist revolution to sue in U.S. courts foreign companies or individuals that "traffic" in property confiscated by the government of President Fidel Castro.
It also allows U.S. visas to be denied shareholders and officers of foreign firms operating these properties in Cuba.

Lage said it was inconceivable that in the United States an "alienated ultra-right wing, allied with a fascist minority of the Cuban exile community, should dictate the policy to be pursued with Cuba."
